sections.heading: The Temptations version
sections.wikitext:
The original Temptations version of "Get Ready", produced by [[Smokey Robinson]], was designed as an answer to the latest dance craze, "The Duck". The Temptations' [[falsetto]] [[Eddie Kendricks]] sings lead on the song, which Robinson produced as an up-tempo dance number with a prominent rhythm provided by Motown drummer [[Benny Benjamin]]. The song made it to No. 1 on the [[United States|U.S.]] [[R&B singles chart]], while peaking at No. 29 on the pop charts.<ref>{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942-2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=571}}</ref>

The [[B-side]] to "Get Ready" was the ballad "Fading Away", which was also led by Kendricks. Written by [[The Miracles]] members Smokey Robinson, [[Warren "Pete" Moore|Pete Moore]], and [[Bobby Rogers]], and produced by Robinson, "Fading Away" was later included on the Temptations 1966 album ''[[Gettin' Ready]]'' along with the hit side.

The group's previous singles since "[[My Girl (The Temptations song)|My Girl]]" had all landed in the U.S. Pop charts (and R&B charts) Top 20. However, although it hit No. 1 on the R&B charts (their first since "My Girl"),  "Get Ready" was only a Top 30 hit (missing the Top 20 by nine positions), while "Fading Away" missed all U.S. national charts. As was promised, the next single released would have Norman Whitfield's song on it. When Whitfield's "[[Ain't Too Proud to Beg]]" (also a No. 1 R&B hit) made it to thirteen on the pop charts, Motown chief [[Berry Gordy]] assigned him to be the Temptations' new main producer. "Get Ready" did eventually become a Top 10 pop hit, but not by the Temptations, but by the Motown rock band [[Rare Earth (band)|Rare Earth]]. (The Temptations' version reached No. 10 in the UK in 1969.)

Until the group recorded "[[Please Return Your Love to Me]]" in 1968, this was their last song to feature lead vocals solely by Kendricks, as [[David Ruffin]] (who was with the group at the time), and later, [[Dennis Edwards]], would be placed in that role in later songs.

The Temptations re-recorded the song as part of a series of promos for American television network [[CBS]] during the 1990-91 TV season. The network had been using the "Get Ready for CBS" tagline since 1988, and the song's lyrics were modified to incorporate the tagline.

2:46 (single version) | label = [[Motown Records|Rare Earth]]
R 5012 | writer = [[Smokey Robinson]] | producer = Rare Earth | prev_title = Generation, Light Up the Sky | prev_year = 1969 | next_title = [[(I Know) I'm Losing You]] | next_year = 1970 }} The [[rock music|rock]] band [[Rare Earth (band)|Rare Earth]] regularly played "Get Ready" in concert, where it was a popular staple of their live performances, and recorded a version for their 1968 [[Verve Records|Verve]] release, ''Dreams/Answers''.{{cite book |last=Betts |first=Graham |date= June 2, 2014 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RG_LAwAAQBAJ&pg=PT187 |title=Motown Encyclopedia |publisher=AC Publishing|page=187 |isbn=9781311441546}} After signing with [[Motown]], executive Barney Ales asked the band to re-record the song for [[Get Ready (Rare Earth album)|their first release]] on Motown's then-unnamed rock subsidiary, due to the audience response to the band's [[cover version|cover]]. After recording a version which was scrapped, the band themselves set up their own recording equipment and recorded a 21-minute version, which later had audience applause dubbed in. The new recording of "Get Ready" was edited down to 2:46 for a single, which was given a Tamla Motown release in the UK, the only release by the band to appear on Motown itself, and unlike the Temptations' version, Rare Earth's recording was a success on the pop chart. The single peaked at #4 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart in 1970.{{cite web |url=http://www.billboard.com/artist/362431/rare-earth/chart |title=Rare Earth - Chart history |publisher=[[Billboard.com]] |accessdate=November 21, 2016}} The Rare Earth version of the song also peaked at number twenty on the R&B chart.{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942-2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=482}} Rare Earth's version of "Get Ready" was routinely used by [[hip hop music|hip hop]] artist [[DJ Kool Herc]] in [[turntablism]] performances.{{cite book |last= Weingarten|first=Christopher R. |title=Public Enemy's It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back |date=8 April 2010 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=_kjTG00KtJ0C&pg=PA20 |publisher=Bloomsbury Academic |page=20 |isbn=9780826429131}} Pioneering hip hop journalist Steven Hager wrote that Rare Earth's recording "was a favorite in the Bronx because it lasted over twenty-one minutes, which was long enough for the serious dancers to get into the beat. They loved to wait for the song's two-minute drum solo to show their most spectacular moves."{{cite book |last=Chang |first=Jeff |date=April 2007 |title=Can't Stop Won't Stop: A History of the Hip-Hop Generation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LwaXZpD11ukC&pg=PA76 |publisher=[[St. Martin's Press]] |page=76 |isbn=9781429902694}}

R 5012 | writer = Smokey Robinson | producer = Rare Earth | prev_title = Generation, Light Up the Sky | prev_year = 1969 | next_title = (I Know) I'm Losing You | next_year = 1970 }} The rock band Rare Earth regularly played "Get Ready" in concert, where it was a popular staple of their live performances, and recorded a version for their 1968 Verve release, Dreams/Answers. After signing with Motown, executive Barney Ales asked the band to re-record the song for their first release on Motown's then-unnamed rock subsidiary, due to the audience response to the band's cover. After recording a version which was scrapped, the band themselves set up their own recording equipment and recorded a 21-minute version, which later had audience applause dubbed in. The new recording of "Get Ready" was edited down to 2:46 for a single, which was given a Tamla Motown release in the UK, the only release by the band to appear on Motown itself, and unlike the Temptations' version, Rare Earth's recording was a success on the pop chart. The single peaked at #4 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart in 1970. The Rare Earth version of the song also peaked at number twenty on the R&B chart. Rare Earth's version of "Get Ready" was routinely used by hip hop artist DJ Kool Herc in turntablism performances. Pioneering hip hop journalist Steven Hager wrote that Rare Earth's recording "was a favorite in the Bronx because it lasted over twenty-one minutes, which was long enough for the serious dancers to get into the beat. They loved to wait for the song's two-minute drum solo to show their most spectacular moves."

sections.heading: Certifications
Other cover versions
sections.wikitext:
* The song was [[Ella Fitzgerald]]'s last US chart record (1969), reaching the ''Billboard'' [[Bubbling Under the Hot 100]] survey (#126)<ref>Joel Whitburn's Bubbling Under the Billboard Hot 100 1959-2004</ref> and the ''Record World'' "Non-Rock Top 40". She performed it on ''[[The Carol Burnett Show]]'' in November 1969.
* Australian singer [[Carol Hitchcock]] released a version which was produced by [[Stock, Aitken and Waterman]] in 1987 that became a moderate hit in her homeland, peaking at No. 18,<ref>{{cite book|last=Kent|first=David|author-link=David Kent (historian)|title=Australian Chart Book 1970–1992|publisher=Australian Chart Book|location=St. Ives, N.S.W.|year=1993|edition=Illustrated|page=139|isbn=0-646-11917-6}} N.B. The Kent Report chart was licensed by [[Australian Recording Industry Association|ARIA]] between mid-1983 and June 19, 1988.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://i.imgur.com/c4eXmKJ.jpg|title=Australian Top 50 ARIA Singles Chart – Week Ending 9th August, 1987|publisher=Imgur.com (original document published by [[Australian Recording Industry Association|ARIA]])|access-date=2017-07-18}}</ref> but only achieved minor UK success, peaking at No. 56.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.officialcharts.com/artist/24229/carol-hitchcock/|title=Official Charts > Carol Hitchcock|publisher=[[Official Charts Company|The Official UK Charts Company]]|access-date=2017-07-18}}</ref>
* The song was recorded by its original author Smokey Robinson, for his 1979 album ''Where There's Smoke…''. This 6-minute disco version was also released as a single and made #82 on the R&B Charts.
* The group again re-recorded the song from their 1991 album, ''[[Milestone (The Temptations album)|Milestone]]'' as a dance version to the original recording.
* Scottish band The Proclaimers recorded a version of the song for the soundtrack of Dumb and Dumber (1994).
